analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-based public health plan anyone can buy and expands premium subsidies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, despite 13 Senate Democrats backing it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates 'Medicare Part E,' a government-run health plan that any U.S. resident could buy through the insurance exchanges, and that employers large and small could offer to workers as an alternative to private plans. It also makes ACA premium subsidies more generous by basing them on mid-tier 'gold' plans and removing the income ceiling on who qualifies, adds cost-sharing help for people up to four times the poverty line, creates a $30 billion fund to reduce out-of-pocket costs, and imposes the first-ever annual cap ($6,700 starting 2026) on what traditional Medicare beneficiaries pay out of pocket. It would also require the plan to cover abortion and reproductive services regardless of state bans.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own health coverage (who would get bigger subsidies and richer gold-level plans), workers at companies that don't offer affordable insurance, traditional Medicare beneficiaries (who would get an annual out-of-pocket limit for the first time), and people in states that restrict abortion coverage, since the plan's reproductive coverage would override state bans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurance buyers, Medicare users, uncovered workers

how_it_helps.text: Creates Medicare Part E public plans available in the individual, small group, and large group markets, sold through the exchanges and offered voluntarily to all employers, with gold-level coverage including all Medicare-covered services.
Requires the public plan to cover abortion and all reproductive services, and bars states from prohibiting that coverage.
Bases ACA premium tax credits on the second-lowest-cost gold plan instead of silver, and permanently removes the 400%-of-poverty income cap on subsidy eligibility.
Extends enhanced cost-sharing reductions (extra help with deductibles and copays) up to 400% of the poverty line, and authorizes funding to expand navigator capacity.
Imposes the first annual out-of-pocket cap on traditional Medicare beneficiaries — $6,700 in 2026, adjusted for medical inflation thereafter.
Appropriates $30 billion for fiscal 2025–2027 for a state reinsurance and affordability fund to lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs, plus $2 billion in startup funding for the public plans.

Requires employers that don't offer affordable coverage to refer full-time employees to exchange navigators, and strengthens federal and state rate review of insurer rates, including for grandfathered plans.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the startup money, the $30 billion affordability fund, and the permanently expanded premium subsidies. Private insurers would compete against a government-run plan in every market they sell in. Hospitals, doctors, and drug makers would face payment rates capped between Medicare and average exchange rates, mandatory network participation for Medicare providers, limits on balance billing, and application of Medicare drug-price negotiation.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $2 billion in startup funding and $30 billion for a reinsurance and affordability fund, and permanently expands premium subsidies with no specified spending offsets, adding to federal deficits.

The public plan must pay providers rates no higher than the average paid by exchange plans and must apply Medicare's balance-billing limits, with all Medicare-participating providers automatically in network — payment levels well below typical commercial rates, which hospitals and physician groups said would strain health system finances.

The plan competes directly with private insurers in the individual, small group, and large group markets, which the insurance industry argued would destabilize private coverage; insurer revenues would also depend partly on the temporary three-year reinsurance fund.
The reproductive-coverage mandate would preempt any state law restricting such coverage — a provision that guaranteed strong opposition in states with bans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer gains are large and concrete: richer subsidies with no income ceiling, lower cost-sharing, a public option in every market, and a first-ever out-of-pocket cap for Medicare beneficiaries. The costs are real but one-sided in design: the bill pays for its affordability fund and startup costs with direct appropriations and leaves the expanded subsidies unoffset, while the burden of lower rates falls on insurers, hospitals, and drug makers rather than being quantified. An honest reading is that this is a substantial expansion of public support for coverage whose financing questions were never worked through, in part because the bill never advanced far enough for committees to revise it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley and 12 Democratic colleagues introduced the Choose Medicare Act on May 1, 2024.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the bill's last action.
All 12 cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican signed on.

The bill text would establish Medicare Part E public plans in the individual, small group, and large group markets, expand premium credits to a gold-plan benchmark and lift the 400%-of-poverty income cap, cap traditional Medicare out-of-pocket costs at $6,700 starting in 2026, and appropriate $30 billion for state reinsurance and affordability programs.
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, hospital and physician groups, and brand-name drug makers are better off, since none of them ever had to compete with the public plan or accept its payment rates. Consumers who would have qualified for bigger subsidies or the Medicare out-of-pocket cap remain under the prior rules.

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 12 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Industry facing a new government-run competitor
against.what_they_did: Opposed public-option legislation, arguing a Medicare-based plan would undercut and crowd out private coverage.

against.name: Hospital, physician, and pharmaceutical industries
against.role: Healthcare provider and drug industries facing lower payment rates
against.what_they_did: Opposed public-option and Medicare payment-rate proposals, citing rates below commercial levels and expanded drug-price negotiation.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats out of a 48-member caucus; no Republican supported it, and with Republicans holding the House the bill had no path forward.

industries.note: The bill puts a government-run plan in direct competition with private insurers in the individual, small group, and large group markets, threatening their premium revenue. A $30 billion reinsurance fund for fiscal 2025–2027 partially cushions them, but it is temporary while the competitor is permanent.

Part E rates are capped between Medicare and average exchange-plan rates — below typical commercial payments — and every Medicare-participating provider is automatically in network, with Medicare's balance-billing limits applying.
The bill applies Medicare's prescription drug negotiation provisions to Part E plans and extends the excise tax penalty for drug makers that fail to negotiate.
All employers would be offered a voluntary Medicare-based option for their workers, with CMS available as a third-party administrator, giving them another lever to hold down coverage costs.
